summary: This EPA web page explains how paper is made and recycled, describing the fiber sources used in paper making and the three basic types of mills: pulp mills, recycled paper processing mills, and mills using both recycled and virgin fiber. It details chemical and mechanical pulping, bleaching, sheet forming and drying, and the deinking and fiber-length limits of recycled paper processing. Navigation and boilerplate are omitted.
one_line: EPA overview of paper making from pulp and recovered fiber, covering the three mill types and how recycled fiber is processed.
key_facts: Today fiber for paper comes mainly from two sources: wood and recycled paper products.
There are three basic types of paper mills: pulp mills, recycled paper processing mills, and mills that use both recycled and virgin fiber.
In chemical pulping, wood chips are cooked in a digester at elevated pressure with chemicals that dissolve lignin.
Chemical pulping is the most common pulping process in the United States.
Mechanical pulping does not use chemicals to remove lignin; wood chips are pressed against a grinder that physically separates the fibers.
Chemical pulps tend to have longer fibers and make strong paper such as printing and writing papers and paperboard.
Mechanical pulps have shorter fibers and produce papers that do not require as much strength, such as newsprint.
To produce white paper, the mill must bleach the pulp using chemicals such as chlorine dioxide, oxygen, or hydrogen peroxide.
In recycled paper processing mills, recovered paper is combined with water in a large vessel called a pulper.
Deinking processes use soaps or surfactants to wash or float ink and other particles away from the fiber.
It is generally accepted that a fiber can be used five to seven times before it becomes too short to be useable in new paper products.
Recovered paper with long fibers, such as office paper, is generally of higher value than recovered paper with short fibers, such as newspaper.
Some mills use both recycled and virgin fiber, typically by adding bales of recycled pulp to wood pulp.
Customer demand, environmental awareness, and economics are reasons mills add recovered fiber to their products.
